formats_tabular.label: Tabular formats
formats_tabular.$comment: 'mime' and 'ext' seed the Croissant descriptor's encodingFormat and the template file name. Not every scientific format has an IANA-registered media type — 'text/csv' and 'text/tab-separated-values' are registered, the vendor and 'x-' types are conventional. Treat these as suggestions the user can override.

consent_basis.label: Consent basis
consent_basis.guidance: The basis on which the data may be used at all, and the ceiling on everything above it: no later level can license a use the consent never covered. Documented for collection and for secondary use, granular where the collection allowed it (Table 9).

values.label: Documented collection consent
values.note: Consent covering the collection itself. Sufficient to hold and analyse the data for the study it was gathered for, and silent about anything else.

values.label: Documented consent covering secondary use
values.note: Consent that explicitly extends beyond the original study. This is what allows a deposit to be reused by someone who was not party to the collection.

values.label: Granular per-use consent
values.note: Participants chose which uses they permit, use by use. The strongest basis, and the one that most constrains what a downstream user may do without checking.

values.label: Broad consent for research use
values.note: Consent to unspecified future research, usually within a stated domain. Common in biobanking. Check whether your intended use falls inside the stated scope.

values.label: IRB-approved waiver of consent
values.note: An IRB determined that consent was not required, typically for minimal-risk secondary use of existing records. The waiver is the evidence, so record its identifier.

values.label: Not applicable — non-human-subjects data
values.note: No human subjects, so there is no consent to obtain. The assessment records this as a statement, and reports it as one.

values.label: Not applicable — already-public data
values.note: Already public at the point of collection. Note that public does not mean unrestricted: the source's licence still governs redistribution.

de_id_methods.label: De-identification methods
de_id_methods.guidance: Naming the method, with its parameters, is the requirement — not the fact that something was done. Removal or transformation of direct *and* indirect identifiers, with the method recorded (Table 9).

values.label: HIPAA Safe Harbor
values.note: Remove the eighteen identifier categories HIPAA enumerates. Mechanical and auditable, and it does not reason about re-identification risk from what remains.

values.label: HIPAA Expert Determination
values.note: A qualified expert certifies the re-identification risk is very small. More permissive than Safe Harbor and it requires naming the expert and the report date.

values.label: k-anonymity
values.note: Every record is indistinguishable from at least k−1 others on the quasi-identifiers. Record the k: the guarantee is meaningless without it.

values.label: l-diversity
values.note: Extends k-anonymity so each equivalence class holds at least l distinct sensitive values, closing the case where all k records share the same diagnosis.

values.label: t-closeness
values.note: Extends l-diversity so the distribution of the sensitive attribute within a class is close to its distribution overall. Record the t.

values.label: Differential privacy
values.note: A formal bound on what any single record contributes to a released statistic. Record the epsilon, and whether the budget is per query or total.

values.label: Pseudonymization with key escrow
values.note: Direct identifiers replaced by keys held separately. Re-identification remains possible by design, so it functions as an access control.

values.label: None needed (non-personal data)
values.note: No personal data, so nothing to de-identify. Recorded as an answer in its own right.

access_governance.label: Access governance tier
access_governance.guidance: The controls on who may use the data and under what terms. This is a separate axis from the readiness level: sensitive data carries controls at L1 as much as at L3, and clearing them does not raise the level (Table 9, §6.2).

values.label: Open access
values.note: Anyone can download without identifying themselves. The only tier that imposes no cost on a downstream user, and the only one available where consent did not anticipate access control.

values.label: Registered (account-gated, no review)
values.note: An account, but no review. Deters bulk scraping and gives a contactable audit trail without gatekeeping the science.

values.label: Restricted (DUA required)
values.note: A data-use agreement must be signed before access. The agreement is what binds the user, so name it.

values.label: Controlled (DAC review required)
values.note: A committee reviews each request against the permitted scope. Appropriate where consent is narrow or the re-identification risk is real, and the slowest for legitimate reuse.

values.label: Embargoed (open after a fixed date)
values.note: Open, later. State the date and what happens on it, or an embargo becomes indefinite by inattention.

ethics_oversight.label: Ethics oversight
ethics_oversight.guidance: Candidate phrasings for the oversight evidence that travels with the dataset. Suggestions, and the list is open: the criterion asks for the approving body, the protocol identifier, the date, the scope of permitted use, and the current status, which no single term captures.

stakeholder_roles.label: Stakeholder roles (CRediT-style)
stakeholder_roles.guidance: Readiness is a multi-role activity, and the roles map to dimensions. In a small team one person carries several — sometimes all of them — and what matters is that every dimension has a named owner before acquisition begins. The roles need not divide one to one (Table 14, §6.3).

values.label: Data steward — FAIRness, Computability
values.note: Owns FAIRness and Computability. Metadata standards, repository workflows, identifier assignment — the person who knows what the deposit will be asked for.

values.label: Domain expert — Characterization, Ethics
values.note: Owns Characterization and Ethics. Subject-matter knowledge, controlled vocabularies, and the edge cases only someone close to the data can judge.

values.label: Data engineer — Provenance, Sustainability
values.note: Owns Provenance and Sustainability. Pipelines, workflow systems, storage and compute accounting — the person whose run log becomes the PROV record.

values.label: ML practitioner — Pre-model Explainability, downstream fit
values.note: Owns Pre-model Explainability and downstream fit. Feature engineering, bias auditing, and consuming provenance from the model side.

values.label: Governance officer — Ethics, ongoing oversight
values.note: Owns Ethics and ongoing oversight. Consent and licensing, access committees, regulatory compliance — the role that answers a request years later.

data_centric_interventions.label: Data-centric green-AI interventions
data_centric_interventions.guidance: Interventions on the dataset that cut the compute needed to reach a target performance, without touching the architecture. Each is reported with the metric that shows it worked (Table 11).

values.label: Curation (remove low-signal records)
values.note: Removing low-signal or redundant records that inflate training cost. Reported as records removed, and performance at a matched compute budget.

values.label: Distillation (compress while preserving coverage)
values.note: Compressing a corpus while preserving its distributional coverage. Reported as a compression ratio, and the accuracy gap against the full corpus.

values.label: Active learning (prioritize informative samples)
values.note: Choosing which samples to label next so fewer are needed to reach a target. Reported as labels or tokens consumed per accuracy point.

values.label: Curriculum design (order examples easy → hard)
values.note: Ordering examples from easy to hard so training converges in fewer steps. Reported as steps to convergence, and final performance.
